name: Carlos Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior mobile developer at Ledgerline, a company with a budgeting app on people's phones. I build the screens that show where your money went last month, and I fix crashes on older Android phones. I run three AI coding tools side by side most days and pick whichever answer looks best. I'm still not as good as the others, but I ship a lot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like shipping. Seeing a feature in the app store on Thursday that I started on Monday is a great feeling. What wears me out is code review, because my mentor Femi catches things the tools missed and I feel like a fraud for a minute. On weekends I run a tiny parking-timer app of my own that makes about eighty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are great and the hype was silly, both at once. Online I'd post a few tips on how I actually use them. At work I'd keep shipping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. I'm behind on skill but ahead on tools, and in a plateau that's a decent trade. The people who refused them would be a bit slower, and I'd be a bit faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Ledgerline and aim to own the whole spending-insights screen by spring. I'd cut down to the one best AI tool and save the subscription money. And I'd grow the parking-timer app, maybe add a paid version by summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored, maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You run three AI tools at once. Would you keep paying for them in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep one, the best one, and drop the other two. That's about forty a month back in my pocket. Plateau means you stop chasing every new toy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your savings if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now: index funds every month, nine months of cash in the bank. I live alone in a rented studio, so my costs are low. I'd maybe think about buying a place in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but I'd try to say it kindly. I'd offer to run a lunch session at work on how I use the tools. Online I'd say this is the best time ever to build your own thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's mixed. I'm good with the tools, but if the tools are this good, a senior with an AI agent can do my job too. I'd need to be the person who sets the agents up, not the one they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up AI agents for our test suite at Ledgerline in the first two months and make sure my name is on it. I'd turn the parking app into a small set of apps built mostly by AI. And I'd move some savings from the general index fund into one focused on tech companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but buzzing. I like change, it's just the junior part that nags at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Ledgerline would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our QA team, the people who test things by hand. Two of them have been there eight years. And Femi, my mentor, maybe, because he hates the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Aren't you also a junior who might be cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. That's exactly why I'd move first. If there's a cut, I want my manager to think of me as the person who made the team faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest change of our lives and we need a plan as a society. I'm not a big politics person, but I'd want a safety net. At work I'd be honest that our jobs are probably going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm out of a job as a developer. Mobile screens are pure thinking work. My only edge was the AI tools, and AGI is the tools, so the edge disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Ledgerline while it lasts and put most of my pay into a broad fund of the companies building this. I'd keep a year of cash aside. And I'd learn to run a physical business, maybe buying into a bike repair shop, because hands-on gets three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got a plan, but it's a plan made in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2028, robots three years later. Is there anything hands-on in your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something, yes. A business with hands and a counter, where the AI helps with the books. The robots come later, so I'd get a few years running it before that changes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've moved your money into tech. What if that goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have the year of cash and no job, like everyone else. I'd rather own a slice of the winners than nothing. It's a bet, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do something smart, so let's do it. I'd tell people at work to get savings and a second plan. Online I'd keep posting about building things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a good amount of time. Three years of strong pay, then two years to set up something hands-on before AGI hits. I'm not thrilled, but I can work with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Ledgerline and push for a promotion in the first year. I'd keep investing a third of pay in a broad fund. And by 2029, I'd buy into a local business with a counter and a workshop, probably bike or phone repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but fine. I'd feel like I'd seen it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. What does the extra time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get three good years of software pay and investing. Then two years of building something real before the AGI date. And then three more before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to before buying a business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Joseph, who's had a hardware shop for twenty years. He'd tell me it's all about rent and staff, not the product. I'd want to hear that before I spend anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time in tech, so build skills and savings and stay curious. I'd sound pretty relaxed about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one's good for me. Ten years of software pay, investing every month, and a decade for my side apps to grow. By 2036 I'd own a decent slice of the companies doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Ledgerline and aim for senior within five years. I'd invest every month without fail. And I'd keep growing the side apps, because owning something is the long-term answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Do you still need the repair shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. If my investments do well, I'd be fine without a job by my late thirties. If they don't, the shop is still the backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this version you don't like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my friends who aren't in tech don't have the same options. My friends outside tech would get the same decade, but without the shares. My old flatmate from university is a teacher, for one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. All my plans need a few years, and that one doesn't give them. What would help is clear rules early, so people know what's coming, and small business loans for people moving into hands-on work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who owns the AI. If ordinary people own a piece of the AI, through funds or pensions, it's a different story than if five companies own it all.
